categories.answer: The voted school budget is the general fund. Every fund together spent $29,929,041 in FY2026, $3,641,567 more, and these pages show where it came from and which lines it paid.

groups.title: Who grants and fees pay for

categories.title: The whole school budget

categories.answer: Buses are getting more expensive, in special education and in the regular-route contract. The state repays only a slice of special education busing. The athletic line rose because the district moved that cost from player fees to the town budget, mostly taxes.
categories.title: School bus costs

categories.answer: Athletics is paid from two pots, the town budget and a fee fund. The town’s ledger shows $463,034 spent in FY2026 and the fee fund $146,911; the district’s own sheets disagree on what each team costs, by a multiple.
categories.title: Athletics costs

categories.answer: Out-of-district tuition was $1,205,949 in FY2025, and 39.3% of it was paid outside the general fund. The state repaid $579,142 in FY2026 through the circuit breaker, a year after the costs.
categories.title: Special education costs

categories.answer: 1,568 children were in Lunenburg’s schools in FY2026, near where the count has sat since FY2015. Another 177 residents were schooled in other public districts, 97 of them at Monty Tech.

elsewhere.title: The departure scenario, with its dials

categories.title: Students and schools

categories.answer: A special education line spent past its vote in 13 of 17 years, on top of the state repayment the vote counts on. A median bad year of the last five ran $116,811 over; the worst year on record, $223,774. Held once, a reserve costs less than a yearly cushion.

groups.title: How big, and why a reserve

categories.title: Special education reserve fund

categories.answer: The state counted 103.4 teacher FTE in FY2026; whether that is a rise or a fall depends on the year it is measured from. Paraprofessional FTE was 67.0 in FY2025, the most per pupil on the state’s sheet. Nothing published says which posts were filled.
categories.title: School staff

categories.answer: Chapter 70 was $9,229,410 of the $11,244,422 the state’s cherry sheet gave Lunenburg for FY2026. All of that year’s rise was the Legislature’s $150-a-pupil minimum; the formula itself added $0.
categories.title: Chapter 70 aid

categories.answer: Lunenburg spent $18,027 a pupil in FY2025, all funds, against a state median of $23,520, and has sat in the state’s bottom quarter for 17 years. Its school general fund spent under its revised budget every year from FY2010 to FY2026.
categories.title: Spending compared

categories.answer: Lunenburg High ran more classes in SY2025 than in SY2017, but a smaller share takes a language or history. Most announced cuts cannot be checked against any published count, and most budget lines cut to zero came back.
categories.title: Programs and cuts

categories.answer: From FY2008 to FY2024 net school spending rose 12.7% after inflation (61.3% as printed), while pupils fell 13.4% and teacher FTE 4.6%. None of it says why.
categories.title: School spending history

categories.answer: Building upkeep’s budget nearly doubled in four years, $332,016 to $652,033, while spending grew 42%. These pages show what it buys, and where the difference sits.
categories.title: Building upkeep

categories.answer: The state certified $3,354,370 of free cash as of 1 July 2025, the most the Town’s records list; 66.1% of the free cash identified that year was money appropriated and not spent.
categories.title: Free cash

categories.answer: The town holds $9,061,421 in nine stabilization accounts as of 1 July 2025. Only the general fund’s $3,147,179 may be spent on anything lawful.
categories.title: Stabilization funds

categories.answer: Town Meeting voted $44,024,349 across twelve groups for FY2025; the schools are 57.1%. Ranked by dollars past the 2.5% levy cap, employee benefits push the budget hardest, then the schools.
categories.title: Town departments

categories.answer: About 11,804 residents live in 4,529 households, 81.3% owner-occupied, on a Census sample. The average single-family bill was $7,444 in FY2026, and the town has 773 more single-family homes than in FY1994 while enrolment fell.

elsewhere.title: Growth dials: what building would have to do

categories.title: Homes, taxes, growth

categories.answer: The town budgeted $3,713,520 for its insurance department in FY2026, and the schools $3,701,195 on their own health line. The department grew 4.3% a year from FY2011, against a 2.5% levy cap.
categories.title: Health insurance costs

categories.answer: Across every board, 66% of FY2023 to FY2026 meetings have minutes listed on the town’s site. In FY2025, 87% of the seats the boards state had a name printed, and the median body changes 32% of its seats a year.
categories.title: Boards and committees

categories.answer: Town Meeting voted the Parks department $134,434 for FY2026. Beside it, a fee fund held $84,818 at 31 March 2026, and rent for school fields goes to a school fund. Neither fund is part of the vote.
categories.title: Parks department

categories.answer: On our projection the school budget is $932,664 short in FY2028 and short every year after: keeping today’s schools costs 5.18% more each year, while revenue grows 3.22% a year and slows. A cut lowers the cost line once; only a rate changes where it heads.
categories.title: The structural gap

categories.answer: Against a projected FY2028 gap of $932,664 (ours), each option has a size and a payer: an override, fees, cuts to programmes or positions, reserves, or the next teachers’ settlement.
categories.title: Closing the gap

categories.answer: Monty Tech is the regional vocational high school Lunenburg belongs to. Lunenburg’s bill was $1,334,521, most of it a minimum the state sets; the school spent $25,827 a pupil in FY2025, less than most vocational districts.
categories.title: Monty Tech finances

categories.answer: Harvard, the district The Bromfield School belongs to, spent $25,565 a pupil in FY2025, $7,538 more than Lunenburg, on the same state measure. It serves a smaller low-income share, and nothing here shows the spending causes results.
categories.title: Harvard and Bromfield

categories.answer: The school general fund closed FY2026 with $482,118 unspent, 1.8% of its budget, at period 13. Town departments stood $858,462 under in June, before their close.

town-headcount-coverage.finding: 6 of the 12 budget groups have a published staff count behind them; one department with a budget has none.
town-headcount-coverage.title: Budgets without headcounts

town-library.finding: The library was voted $583,890 for FY2025, 1.3% of the budget, growing 8.8% a year.
town-library.title: Library budget

town-population.finding: About 11,804 residents in 4,529 households, on a sample; both grew by more than the survey’s margin.
town-population.title: Population and households

town-public-safety.finding: Police, fire and the inspectors were voted $4,643,717 for FY2025, 10.5% of the budget.
town-public-safety.title: Police, fire and inspectors

town-public-works.finding: Public works grew 2.9% a year, close to the cap; one line rose more than the whole group.
town-public-works.title: Public works

town-schools-line.finding: The schools are 57.1% of the voted budget and grew 3.6% a year, FY2023 to FY2025.
town-schools-line.title: Schools in the omnibus

town-smaller-departments.finding: Veterans and elder services, health, and central purchasing are 1.2% of the budget together.
town-smaller-departments.title: Smaller departments

town-solid-waste.finding: Trash and recycling grew 22.6% a year, the fastest of the twelve, from $312,634 to $469,775.
town-solid-waste.title: Trash and recycling

town-staff-counts.finding: 8 town departments print a staff count, in 7 different forms that cannot be added up.
town-staff-counts.title: Town staff counts

town-voted-total.finding: The voted total was $44,024,349 for FY2025 and $49,374,465 for FY2026, a 12.2% rise.
town-voted-total.title: Voted budget total

tuition-budget.finding: FY2027 budgets out-of-district tuition at $700,142, $591,151 below FY2026, a 46% cut.
tuition-budget.title: Tuition budget

turf-field-capital-plans.finding: The schools have put the field in every capital plan of theirs since FY2022; its year kept moving.
turf-field-capital-plans.title: Turf field capital plans

unpriced-school-charges.finding: Nine charges a Lunenburg family can meet have no published amount anywhere in this archive.
unpriced-school-charges.title: Unpriced school charges

unspent-by-fund.finding: Fees, lunch and the circuit breaker held $1,692,438 at the end of FY2023; by our count, $1,119,636 by FY2026.

related.title: Carried-over orders
related.why: Open orders carried from one year into the next

related.title: Budget lines, all funds
related.why: Every budget line, with what all funds spent on it

unspent-by-fund.title: Unspent money by fund

upkeep-budget-vs-spending.finding: Building upkeep’s budget rose 96% from FY2023 to FY2026; what it spent rose 42%.
upkeep-budget-vs-spending.title: Upkeep budget and spending

upkeep-ledger.finding: Building upkeep left $195,934 in FY2026 on 14 accounts; each card shows what was paid, skipped and released.
upkeep-ledger.title: Upkeep leftover by account

upkeep-skipped.finding: 10 payees the schools used every year were paid under half as usual in FY2026; 5 got nothing.
upkeep-skipped.title: Usual purchases skipped

upkeep-spending.finding: Most of building upkeep is steady work: $291,136 to $389,138 a year to payees paid year after year.
upkeep-spending.title: What upkeep buys

upkeep-surplus-every-dollar.finding: Building upkeep left $195,934 in FY2026: $75,660 on one account, the rest on 13 others.
upkeep-surplus-every-dollar.title: Upkeep surplus, every dollar

what-per-pupil-counts.finding: Three official measures of school spending count different things; neither state one counts capital.
what-per-pupil-counts.title: What per pupil counts

who-may-spend-it.finding: Only the general fund, $3,147,179 of $9,061,421, may go to any lawful use, by a two-thirds vote.
who-may-spend-it.title: Who may spend it

world-languages.finding: 57.8% of Lunenburg High took a language in SY2025, against 70.1% in SY2017; the middle school fell further.
world-languages.title: World languages

years-in-the-home.finding: 1,799 ± 297 owner households moved in before 2010, about half; the median owner moved in in 2010.
years-in-the-home.title: Years in the home

youth-league-payments.finding: One league’s field payments are on record: $39,073.50 across 7 receipts, FY2024 to FY2026.
youth-league-payments.title: Youth league payments
